title: Ὄνος ⟨χωλαίνειν προσποιούμενος⟩ καὶ λύκος
titleEn: The Donkey Pretending to Limp and the Wolf
part: The Donkey Pretending to Limp and the Wolf (Chambry 281)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 281. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ὄνος ἔν τινι λειμῶνι νεμόμενος, ὡς ἐθεάσατο λύκον ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ὁρμώμενον, χωλαίνειν προσεποιεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Onos en tini leimōni nemomenos, hōs etheasato lykon ep’ auton hormōmenon, chōlainein prosepoieito.
sentences.l: A donkey grazing in a certain meadow, when he saw a wolf rushing upon him, pretended to limp.
sentences.n: προσποιέομαι with the infinitive is 'to make a show of, pretend to', met before at fable 70. νέμομαι in the middle is what the animal does — to feed itself, graze — where the active is what the herdsman does.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ προσελθόντος αὐτῷ καὶ τὴν αἰτίαν πυνθανομένου δι’ ἣν χωλαίνει, ἔλεγεν ὡς φραγμὸν διαβαίνων σκόλοπα ἐπάτησα καὶ παρῄνει αὐτῷ πρῶτον ἐξελεῖν τὸν σκόλοπα, εἶθ’ οὕτως αὐτὸν καταθοινήσασθαι, ἵνα μὴ ἐσθίων περιπαρῇ.
sentences.tr: Tou de proselthontos autōi kai tēn aitian pynthanomenou di’ hēn chōlainei, elegen hōs phragmon diabainōn skolopa epatēsa kai parēinei autōi prōton exelein ton skolopa, eith’ houtōs auton katathoinēsasthai, hina mē esthiōn periparēi.
sentences.l: And when he had come up to him and was asking the reason on account of which he was limping, he said that, crossing a fence, 'I trod on a thorn', and he advised him first to take the thorn out, and then in that way to make his feast of him, so that he might not be pierced through as he ate.
sentences.i: When the wolf came up and asked why he was limping, the donkey said he had trodden on a thorn while crossing a fence, and urged him to pull the thorn out first and only then make his meal of him, so that he should not be spitted on it as he ate.
sentences.n: ἔλεγεν ὡς opens indirect speech, but the Greek slides into the donkey's own words with the first-person ἐπάτησα, 'I trod on' — a mixture of reported and direct speech that Greek allows and English cannot; the literal line marks the switch, the idiomatic line keeps it all reported. καταθοινάομαι is to make a feast of a thing, the κατα- meaning 'right down, the whole of it'.

sentences.t: Τοῦ δὲ πεισθέντος καὶ τὸν πόδα αὐτοῦ ἐπάραντος ὅλον τε τὸν νοῦν πρὸς τῇ ὁπλῇ ἔχοντος, ὁ ὄνος λὰξ εἰς τὸ στόμα τοὺς ὀδόντας αὐτοῦ ἐτίναξε.
sentences.tr: Tou de peisthentos kai ton poda autou eparantos holon te ton noun pros tēi hoplēi echontos, ho onos lax eis to stoma tous odontas autou etinaxe.
sentences.l: And when he had been persuaded and had lifted up the donkey's foot and was holding his whole mind on the hoof, the donkey with a kick into his mouth shook his teeth.
sentences.i: The wolf was persuaded, and lifted the donkey's foot, and had his whole mind on the hoof; and the donkey kicked him in the mouth and knocked his teeth loose.
sentences.n: One genitive absolute carrying three participles in a row — πεισθέντος, ἐπάραντος, ἔχοντος — which is how the fables hold a whole scene in suspense before the main verb lands. λάξ is an adverb, 'with the heel', the regular word for a kick; τινάσσω is to shake a thing violently.

sentences.t: Καὶ ὃς κακῶς διατεθεὶς ἔφη· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε δίκαια πέπονθα· τί γάρ, τοῦ πατρός με μαγειρικὴν τέχνην διδάξαντος, αὐτὸς ἰατρικῆς ἐπελαβόμην ; »
sentences.tr: Kai hos kakōs diatetheis ephē· « All’ egōge dikaia pepontha· ti gar, tou patros me mageirikēn technēn didaxantos, autos iatrikēs epelabomēn ; »
sentences.l: And he, having been put in a bad state, said: « But I at least have suffered just things; for why, my father having taught me the butcher's art, did I myself take up medicine? »
sentences.i: And the wolf, badly hurt, said: « But it serves me right. Why, when my father taught me the butcher's trade, did I take up doctoring? »
sentences.n: δίκαια πέπονθα, 'I have suffered just things', is the Greek for 'it serves me right'. καὶ ὅς is the old demonstrative use of the relative ὅς, 'and he', a survival kept alive in narrative. μαγειρική is the meat-handler's craft: the corpus renders μάγειρος 'cook' where he is at the fire (178, 183) and 'butcher' where he deals in the meat itself (246), and a wolf's inherited trade is the latter — though 'cook's art' is a defensible reading of the same words.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ μηδὲν προσήκουσιν ἐπιχειροῦντες εἰκότως δυστυχοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi mēden prosēkousin epicheirountes eikotōs dystychousin.
sentences.l: So too, among men, those who set their hand to things that belong to them in nothing fare badly, and with reason.
sentences.i: So too, among men, those who take up what is no business of theirs come to grief, and deservedly.
sentences.n: Almost the same closing as fable 150, which adds a clause about abandoning one's own pursuits. ἐπιχειρέω, 'put one's hand to', takes the dative, and μηδέν is adverbial with the participle προσήκουσιν. εἰκότως is 'as was to be expected'.
